topics.title: Chapter 14 — Logging and the systemd Journal
topics.summary: An incident is often a story told by several partial witnesses. The web server knows the HTTP result, systemd knows the process exit, the kernel knows a storage error, and SSH knows who connected. HarborWorks needs these records to form a timeline without pretending that every message is equally reliable or that events close in time must share a cause.

topics.title: 14.1 Why Logs Matter
topics.summary: A log is a record of an event, ideally including a timestamp, source, severity, and enough context to investigate. Logs answer questions that current process state cannot: what failed earlier, which configuration was loaded, and how a request ended.

blocks.text: A log is a record of an event, ideally including a timestamp, source, severity, and enough context to investigate. Logs answer questions that current process state cannot: what failed earlier, which configuration was loaded, and how a request ended.

Logging also has costs and risks. Excessive volume consumes storage and hides signals; secrets in logs create another credential store. Decide what to record, who may read it, where it goes, how long it remains, and how to detect a broken logging pipeline. A missing message can mean “no event,” “not logged,” “not retained,” or “not collected.”
Linux example — 14.1
Read a bounded log interval.
journalctl -b --since '10 minutes ago' -n 50 --no-pager

topics.title: 14.2 Traditional Linux Logging
topics.summary: Many systems write text logs beneath /var/log, but the exact files depend on installed services and configuration. Debian-family authentication messages often appear in auth.log when a traditional logging daemon is configured; RHEL-family installations commonly use secure. Neither filename is guaranteed on every minimal image.

topics.title: 14.4 rsyslog
topics.summary: rsyslog can receive, filter, transform, store, and forward messages. Its rules and inputs determine the paths. A system using both journald and rsyslog needs a deliberately understood flow to avoid missing messages, duplicate collection, or forwarding loops.

blocks.text: rsyslog can receive, filter, transform, store, and forward messages. Its rules and inputs determine the paths. A system using both journald and rsyslog needs a deliberately understood flow to avoid missing messages, duplicate collection, or forwarding loops.

Validate configuration with the installed daemon’s validation mode, commonly rsyslogd -N1, before applying changes. Reliable forwarding also needs queue behavior, disk capacity, transport security, and receiver health. TCP reduces some transport loss risks compared with basic UDP delivery, but a connected socket alone does not prove durable ingestion. (R34)

sudo rsyslogd -N1

blocks.text: journald collects structured records from sources including service standard output/error, syslog messages, and kernel messages. Fields can identify a unit, process, user, or boot, making filtering more reliable than searching arbitrary text alone.

Journal storage can be volatile under /run or persistent under /var/log/journal, depending on configuration and environment. Storage=auto does not mean every installation retains previous boots. Inspect journald.conf and its drop-ins, storage directories, and actual retained boots. Retention limits and rate limiting affect which evidence remains available. (R33)

blocks.text: -b chooses the current boot; -b -1 selects the previous retained boot when available. -u filters a unit. Priority filtering is useful, but an informational message may contain the key configuration detail, so broaden the query when necessary.

Use -o short-iso-precise for readable timestamps and -o json for structured processing where supported. Access is controlled; running as an ordinary user may show only a subset of records. A permission-limited view is not a complete system history. (R33)

topics.title: 14.7 Kernel Messages
topics.summary: The kernel records events such as device discovery, filesystem errors, and out-of-memory decisions. These can explain why an application failed even when its own log ends abruptly. journalctl -k -b focuses on kernel records retained for the current boot.

blocks.text: The kernel records events such as device discovery, filesystem errors, and out-of-memory decisions. These can explain why an application failed even when its own log ends abruptly. journalctl -k -b focuses on kernel records retained for the current boot.

Preserve the surrounding sequence, not just the last alarming line. A filesystem becoming read-only may be a protective response to an earlier I/O error. Treat the underlying storage problem before attempting to force writes. Correlate device identifiers carefully because names can change across boots.
Linux example — 14.7
Read current-boot kernel messages.
sudo journalctl -k -b -n 50 --no-pager

topics.title: 14.8 dmesg
topics.summary: dmesg reads the kernel ring buffer, subject to access policy. The ring buffer is finite and is not an archive. Older messages can be overwritten, and reading it after reboot does not reconstruct the prior boot.

blocks.text: dmesg reads the kernel ring buffer, subject to access policy. The ring buffer is finite and is not an archive. Older messages can be overwritten, and reading it after reboot does not reconstruct the prior boot.

Human-readable timestamps can be convenient, but conversions around clock changes require care. Compare with journal boot identifiers and wall-clock records when constructing a timeline. topics.title: 14.9 Application Logs
topics.summary: Applications should record outcomes in terms meaningful to the service: request identifiers, status codes, dependency failures, and bounded durations. Standard output/error works naturally with systemd collection, while file logging requires ownership, rotation, and reopen behavior.

blocks.text: Applications should record outcomes in terms meaningful to the service: request identifiers, status codes, dependency failures, and bounded durations. Standard output/error works naturally with systemd collection, while file logging requires ownership, rotation, and reopen behavior.

Avoid logging passwords, bearer tokens, private keys, or unnecessary personal information. Even a URL can carry a secret in its query string. A log line is also untrusted input: attackers or ordinary users can supply strings that imitate severity labels or introduce confusing line breaks. Use structured fields and safe rendering.

topics.title: 14.11 Log Rotation

blocks.text: Rotation limits individual log-file growth and manages retention. logrotate can rename files, compress older copies, and invoke a post-rotation action. The application often must reopen its log so it stops writing through an old descriptor.

The copytruncate approach copies a file then truncates the original, but writes during that sequence can be lost. Prefer a supported reopen mechanism when available. Use logrotate -d CONFIG to inspect proposed behavior without performing a normal rotation. Do not force rotation repeatedly on production logs to test a guess. (R34)

topics.title: 14.12 Centralized Logging
topics.summary: Central collection helps preserve evidence when a host fails and enables cross-host correlation. It needs trustworthy host identity, synchronized clocks, protected transport, access controls, retention, and an ingestion-health signal. A central dashboard cannot compensate for a silent collector.

Design for network interruption. Decide how much local buffering is available, what happens when it fills, and whether loss or application blocking is acceptable. Monitor both the shipping process and the age of the newest received event. “Agent running” is weaker evidence than an end-to-end test message reaching durable storage.
